en.statement: A mutation returns selected data after performing its write.
en.explanation: A mutation combines a write with a fetch of the selected result, so its response can show the state produced by the write.

en.statement: A service executes a document that combines an operation with a type definition.
en.explanation: A document containing a type system definition is unsuitable for execution. The service should return a descriptive error.

en.statement: A lone query with an operation directive qualifies for the `{ ... }` shorthand.
en.explanation: Query shorthand requires a lone query with no variables, operation directives or description.

en.statement: An anonymous query may declare variables when it is the document's single operation.
en.explanation: The lone-anonymous-operation rule permits an unnamed operation when the document contains one operation, even if that operation declares variables.

en.statement: A query and a mutation may share an operation name within one document.
en.explanation: Operation names are unique across the document, including across different operation types.

en.statement: A service runs the first operation when a multi-operation request omits operationName.
en.explanation: A request containing several operations needs operationName to identify one. Omitting it produces a request error.

en.statement: A service collects exactly one root response name per valid subscription operation.
en.explanation: The service collects a subscription's root selections, including fields reached through fragments, and checks that there is one root field.

en.statement: A field named `userName` matches a selection named `username`.
en.explanation: GraphQL treats names with different letter case as different names. A selection has to match the schema's spelling.

en.statement: GraphQL permits Unicode letters such as `é` inside a field name.
en.explanation: Names use ASCII letters, digits and underscores; letters outside the ASCII range are invalid in a name.

en.statement: Adding commas between selections preserves an operation's meaning.
en.explanation: GraphQL treats separator commas as ignored tokens, so developers can use them for readability.

en.statement: In the September 2025 spec, removing an operation description preserves its execution result.
en.explanation: Executable descriptions supply documentation. Removing an operation's description leaves its result unchanged.

en.statement: A field needs an object return type to declare arguments.
en.explanation: Fields returning scalars can declare arguments too, such as a picture field taking a size argument.

en.statement: A repeated argument in a field selection takes its last supplied value.
en.explanation: Repeating an argument name within one field selection is invalid; GraphQL rejects the ambiguity.

en.statement: The alias in `label: name` makes `label` the response name for that result.
en.explanation: An alias supplies the key for a selected field's value in the response object.

en.statement: A client may choose `__label` as the alias for an ordinary field selection.
en.explanation: The reserved prefix restricts schema names, while field aliases have no such restriction.

en.statement: A query may select `item(id: 1)` and `item(id: 2)` under one response name on the same object type.
en.explanation: Selections under the same parent type need identical arguments to share a response name.

en.statement: Selections on distinct object types need matching leaf types to share a response name.
en.explanation: Even mutually exclusive object branches have to produce the same response shape for a shared response name.

en.statement: A service adds unselected scalar fields when it completes a selected object.
en.explanation: The client's selections determine the data fields in the response. Completing an object does not add unselected schema fields.

en.statement: A JSON response to `user { id ...F email }` with `fragment F on User { name }` should list `name` second.
en.explanation: A fragment spread contributes its fields at the spread's position, and a JSON response should keep the response field order textually, so the user object lists id, name, email.

en.statement: A skipped occurrence fixes a field's response order before an included occurrence.
en.explanation: Fields excluded by directives do not count toward response ordering. The first included occurrence determines the position.

en.statement: An operation references `fragment UserBits on User` with the syntax `...UserBits`.
en.explanation: The spread syntax uses three dots followed by the fragment's name to incorporate its field selections.

en.statement: The service checks a fragment's type condition against the runtime object's concrete type.
en.explanation: A fragment applies according to the concrete object returned for that response position.

en.statement: An inline fragment that omits `on Type` takes its type from the enclosing selection set.
en.explanation: An inline fragment's omitted type condition inherits the surrounding type context.

en.statement: One document may hold two definitions of `fragment UserFields`, one for each of its two operations.
en.explanation: Spreads refer to fragment definitions by name, so each fragment name must be unique within the whole document; a second UserFields definition makes it invalid.

en.statement: A document's unused fragment definitions pass validation when their fields match the schema.
en.explanation: A document containing a defined fragment that is never spread fails validation.

source.title: GraphQL Specification: Fragments Must Be Used

en.statement: A fragment spread may use a named fragment defined in another document sent to the same service.
en.explanation: A named fragment spread refers to a fragment definition in the same document.

source.title: GraphQL Specification: Fragment Spread Target Defined

en.statement: A fragment may reach itself again through a spread placed inside one of its child fields.
en.explanation: Fragment spread cycles invalidate the document, including cycles that pass through child fields and other fragments.

source.title: GraphQL Specification: Fragment Spreads Must Not Form Cycles

en.statement: A spread between two interfaces is possible when an object type implements both interfaces.
en.explanation: A shared possible object type gives the parent interface and fragment condition a nonempty intersection.

source.title: GraphQL Specification: Fragment Spread Is Possible

en.statement: An inline fragment declares a name that later fragment spreads can reference.
en.explanation: An inline fragment supplies its selection set at its location and declares no fragment name.

en.statement: Two operations in one document may each declare `$limit` with their own variable type.
en.explanation: Variable-name uniqueness is checked per operation, so separate operations can declare the same name independently.

en.statement: Each operation that reaches a fragment using `$limit` declares `$limit` in its variable definitions.
en.explanation: Variable uses in transitively referenced fragments are checked against the consuming operation's variable definitions.

source.title: GraphQL Specification: All Variable Uses Defined

en.statement: An operation may declare an unused variable when the client supplies a value for it.
en.explanation: An unused variable definition makes an operation invalid. Supplying its value does not create a variable use.

en.statement: The service replaces an explicit null variable value with the variable's declared default.
en.explanation: A variable's default applies when its value is omitted. An explicit null is a supplied value.

en.statement: A variable declared as `$size: Int = 10` is valid at an argument of type `Int!`.
en.explanation: A non-null variable default permits this nullable variable at a non-null argument position.

source.title: GraphQL Specification: All Variable Usages Are Allowed

en.statement: A variable of type `[Int]` passes validation at an argument of type `[Int!]`.
en.explanation: Validation compares declared types. Nullable list items in `[Int]` are incompatible with the non-null items expected by `[Int!]`.

source.title: GraphQL Specification: All Variable Usages Are Allowed

en.statement: A block string turns the characters `\n` into a line break in its input value.
en.explanation: A block string preserves `\n` as a backslash followed by `n` rather than interpreting it as an escape sequence.

en.statement: The service accepts the JSON variable string `"123"` as a value for a variable of type `Int`.
en.explanation: Int input coercion rejects strings with numeric content; `"123"` remains a string input.

en.statement: The service accepts the integer literal `123` as an input value for an argument of type `Float`.
en.explanation: Float input coercion converts an accepted integer input to a floating-point value.

en.statement: The service may accept the JSON variable string `"RED"` for an enum type that defines `RED`.
en.explanation: JSON has no separate enum representation, so a variable string may identify the enum value with that name.

en.statement: The service coerces the integer literal `5` to `[5]` when an argument expects `[Int]`.
en.explanation: List input coercion wraps an accepted single item in a list of length one.

en.statement: The service ignores extra fields supplied in an input object value after reading its defined fields.
en.explanation: An input object value containing a field absent from its expected input type raises a request error.

en.statement: A service with arbitrary-precision integers exposes their full range through Int results.
en.explanation: Int results use the signed 32-bit range regardless of the implementation language. An out-of-range result should raise an execution error.

en.statement: A service returns a resolver's positive Infinity as a successful Float result.
en.explanation: Float results are finite double-precision values. A non-finite internal value such as Infinity raises an execution error.

en.statement: A GraphQL service chooses the internal encoding it uses for its String values.
en.explanation: GraphQL defines String values through Unicode code points. It leaves their in-memory encoding to the service.

en.statement: In the September 2025 spec, a service serializes a numeric ID result as a JSON string.
en.explanation: ID results use JSON string values even when the service stores identifiers as integers. This preserves one serialized form for identifiers.

en.statement: A service may coerce the internal string "123" to the Int result 123.
en.explanation: The service controls scalar result coercion when it preserves information. Parsing the internal string "123" as the integer 123 is an allowed Int result coercion.

en.statement: A scalar named DateTime gets its date format from the GraphQL specification.
en.explanation: The service defines DateTime's format and coercion rules. GraphQL supplies the custom scalar mechanism and lets the service choose the contract.

en.statement: A schema may attach `@specifiedBy(url:)` to the built-in `String` scalar.
en.explanation: The @specifiedBy directive applies to custom scalars. The spec forbids applying it to built-in scalar types.

en.statement: Introspection includes unused built-in scalars in the schema's type list.
en.explanation: Introspection lists a built-in scalar when the schema references it. A built-in scalar with no schema references is omitted from that list.

en.statement: The spec recommends writing enum value names in all caps, such as `READY`.
en.explanation: The all-caps style is a recommendation for schema authors. A name such as READY follows that style.

en.statement: A service serializes an enum result using the numeric value in its internal representation.
en.explanation: A service serializes an enum result as its defined name. Its internal representation stays an implementation detail.

en.statement: A schema must define at least one field on each object type it exposes.
en.explanation: Even an object used merely as a marker needs a field in its schema definition.

en.statement: A schema keeps field names unique within an object type, even when the fields have different argument lists.
en.explanation: GraphQL object fields are identified by their names within the type. Different arguments do not create separate overloads of a field name.

en.statement: An implementing object may return `String!` for an interface field declared as `String`.
en.explanation: Interface field return types permit a subtype. An implementing object's Non-Null String return strengthens the interface's nullable String guarantee.

en.statement: An implementing field may declare `Float` for an argument that its interface field declares as `Int`.
en.explanation: An implementing field must accept each interface argument with the same type (invariant), so an Int argument stays Int; how numeric values coerce plays no part in this schema rule.

en.statement: An implementing object may add a nullable argument to a field declared by its interface.
en.explanation: Interface fields set a minimum argument contract. A nullable extra argument does not demand more input from an existing caller.

en.statement: In the September 2025 spec, an object may deprecate a field whose interface field is left undeprecated.
en.explanation: In the September 2025 spec, an implementing field may be deprecated only when the interface field it implements is deprecated too; otherwise the schema is invalid.

en.statement: A schema joins multiple implemented interfaces with & in an object's SDL declaration.
en.explanation: The implements clause lists interface names separated by &. This lets one object declare that it fulfills several interface contracts.

en.statement: An object automatically declares an ancestor interface by listing an interface that implements it.
en.explanation: An object type's implements clause explicitly includes its transitively implemented interfaces. The service does not infer those declarations from the direct interface alone.

en.statement: A query directly selects an implementer-specific field from an interface result.
en.explanation: The interface declaration determines which fields a query selects directly. An implementer's extra field is reached through a fragment on an applicable type.

en.statement: A union may list an interface member to include that interface's implementing objects.
en.explanation: A union's members are object types. To include several objects that implement an interface, the schema names those objects as members.

en.statement: A query directly selects `name` from a union whose object members define `name`.
en.explanation: Shared object fields do not become union fields. A query reaches name through a fragment on a matching object or interface type.

en.statement: A field of type `[String!]` enforces a non-null value for the whole list.
en.explanation: For `[String!]`, the outer List is nullable, so a null result for the whole list is valid.

source.title: GraphQL Specification: Combining List and Non-Null

en.statement: The service accepts `[]` as the result of a field declared as `[String!]!`.
en.explanation: An empty list satisfies `[String!]!`; these wrappers constrain null values rather than list length.

source.title: GraphQL Specification: Combining List and Non-Null

en.statement: A schema author creates a valid type by wrapping `String!` in another Non-Null wrapper.
en.explanation: A Non-Null wrapper must surround a nullable type. Wrapping an existing Non-Null type again produces an invalid type.

en.statement: A client may omit an argument declared as `limit: Int! = 10` from a field selection.
en.explanation: An argument's schema default makes the argument optional under the Required Arguments rule.

en.statement: The service sets a failed item of an `[Int]` result to null while keeping the other items.
en.explanation: A list with nullable items isolates an item's execution error to that item position.

en.statement: An object field may declare an input object type, such as `ReviewInput`, as its return type.
en.explanation: Input Object types serve input positions. A field's return type must use an output type.

en.statement: A schema author adds arguments to input object fields to configure how the service coerces them.
en.explanation: Input object fields declare input values and take no arguments.

en.statement: A schema author may define an ordinary input object cycle whose chain includes a nullable field.
en.explanation: A nullable link lets a finite input value terminate an ordinary input object's circular chain.

en.statement: The service automatically records an explicitly null nullable field in an ordinary input object's coerced map.
en.explanation: Input object coercion records the provided field name together with null in its resulting map.

en.statement: In the September 2025 spec, an `@oneOf` input may supply a single field whose value is null.
en.explanation: A OneOf Input Object's provided field needs a non-null value. Providing a single field with null fails input coercion.

en.statement: In the September 2025 spec, a schema author must declare OneOf member fields with non-null types.
en.explanation: OneOf fields are declared with nullable types so the client can choose which member to provide.

en.statement: A valid GraphQL schema includes a query root operation type even when clients use the service for mutations.
en.explanation: A query root is a required part of schema validity, including for services whose applications mainly send mutations.

en.statement: A GraphQL schema may use one object type as both its query root and its mutation root.
en.explanation: A schema uses distinct object types for its query and mutation roots. Assigning one type to both roles violates schema validity.

en.statement: In the September 2025 spec, SDL can omit `schema` when default root names accompany a schema description.
en.explanation: A schema description needs an explicit `schema` definition, even when the roots use their default names.

en.statement: In the September 2025 spec, a non-root type named `Mutation` needs an explicit SDL schema definition.
en.explanation: The explicit schema definition prevents SDL from interpreting the ordinary type named `Mutation` as the mutation root.

en.statement: An SDL document may hold both `schema { query: Query }` and `schema { mutation: Mutation }`.
en.explanation: An SDL document holds at most one schema definition; to add a root operation type to a schema already defined, SDL uses an extension such as `extend schema { mutation: Mutation }`.

en.statement: GraphQL gives a schema's object types and input object types a shared namespace for type names.
en.explanation: Type names identify types across the whole schema. An object type and an input object type therefore need different names.

en.statement: A schema may use the same enum type for a field's return value and for an argument's input value.
en.explanation: Enum types qualify for both input and output positions, so one declared enum can serve both uses.

source.title: GraphQL Specification: Input and Output Types

en.statement: An object field may use the schema's query root type directly as its return type.
en.explanation: The query root is an ordinary Object type with an entry-point role. Another object field can use it as an output type.

en.statement: An SDL `extend type` declaration can replace an existing field's return type with a new type.
en.explanation: An object extension adds to the existing type. Its added fields need new names rather than redefining a field already on that type.

en.statement: A client can read the schema's SDL description through introspection at `__schema { description }`.
en.explanation: Schema documentation is available through introspection. `__Schema.description` exposes the description attached to the schema definition.

en.statement: In the September 2025 spec, a client identifies a union membership with a coordinate such as `SearchResult.User`.
en.explanation: Schema coordinates do not identify union memberships. A union member refers to an existing type, whose type coordinate identifies that type.

en.statement: A service honors @skip(if: true) on a query operation by skipping its execution.
en.explanation: QUERY is absent from @skip's declared locations. Attaching @skip to a query operation fails validation.

source.title: GraphQL specification: Directives Are in Valid Locations

en.statement: In the September 2025 spec, a constant @include(if: true) keeps a subscription's root selection valid.
en.explanation: The September 2025 spec forbids @skip and @include in a subscription's root selection set, even when the condition is a literal.

en.statement: In the September 2025 spec, `@deprecated` declares its `reason` argument with type `String!`.
en.explanation: The reason argument of @deprecated has type String! in the September 2025 spec. Supplying null violates that type.

en.statement: In the September 2025 spec, a schema author may place @deprecated on an optional argument definition.
en.explanation: The September 2025 spec includes ARGUMENT_DEFINITION among @deprecated's locations, so schema authors can mark an optional argument as deprecated.

en.statement: In the September 2025 spec, a schema author may apply @deprecated to a required input field.
en.explanation: The @deprecated directive is forbidden on input fields whose types are non-null and which lack defaults. Such a declaration makes the schema invalid.

en.statement: A client may select a deprecated field in an otherwise valid operation.
en.explanation: Deprecation does not remove a field from the schema. Existing clients can continue selecting that field while it remains defined.

en.statement: `directive @x on FIELD_DEFINITION` lets `@x` appear on a field selection.
en.explanation: FIELD_DEFINITION is a type system location for field definitions in SDL; a directive written on a field selection in an operation needs the executable location FIELD.

source.title: GraphQL Specification: Directives Are in Valid Locations

en.statement: The spec guarantees the same semantics after a schema author reverses custom directive order.
en.explanation: Directive order can have semantic meaning. Reversing custom directives can change the schema behavior the service attaches to them.

en.statement: The spec recommends a service-specific prefix for custom directive names.
en.explanation: A prefix reduces collisions between a service's custom directives and future built-ins. The spec says future built-in directive names will omit underscores.

en.statement: A service returns the concrete object's type name for `__typename` inside an interface selection set.
en.explanation: The __typename meta-field reports the actual object type for the current result, rather than the interface type used in the schema.

en.statement: A subscription operation may select __typename as its single root field.
en.explanation: The __typename meta-field is prohibited at the root of a subscription operation. A subscription that selects it there fails validation.

en.statement: A client reaches __schema and __type(name:) as fields of the query root.
en.explanation: These implicit query-root fields expose the service's schema. __type(name:) lets a client look up a particular named type.

en.statement: For a schema supporting queries alone, __Schema.mutationType returns null.
en.explanation: Introspection uses a null mutationType to report that the schema does not support mutations.

en.statement: A service reports the wrapped type's name as __Type.name for a LIST type.
en.explanation: __Type.name is null for LIST and NON_NULL wrappers. A wrapper has a kind rather than a named-type identity.

en.statement: A service returns `NON_NULL` as `ofType.kind` when introspecting the outer wrapper of `[String!]`.
en.explanation: The outer LIST wrapper's ofType points to its immediate item type, String!, so that next type has kind NON_NULL.

en.statement: A service reports null in __Type.interfaces for an object that implements zero interfaces.
en.explanation: For OBJECT and INTERFACE types, __Type.interfaces is a list. An object that implements no interfaces yields an empty list.

en.statement: A service lists concrete object types in __Type.possibleTypes for an interface or union.
en.explanation: __Type.possibleTypes describes the object types that a value of the abstract type can resolve to. Its entries are object types.

en.statement: A service includes deprecated enum values by default when a client selects `__Type.enumValues`.
en.explanation: The includeDeprecated argument defaults to false. A client asks for includeDeprecated: true to include deprecated enum values in this introspection list.

en.statement: A service exposes an Int argument's default as a JSON number in __InputValue.defaultValue.
en.explanation: __InputValue.defaultValue contains a string written in GraphQL syntax. An Int default of 5 appears as the string "5", rather than the number 5.

en.statement: A service returns false from __Directive.isRepeatable when it introspects the @skip directive.
en.explanation: The @skip directive is declared without the repeatable keyword, so its __Directive.isRepeatable value is false.

en.statement: The September 2025 spec recommends sorting introspection's field lists alphabetically.
en.explanation: The September 2025 spec recommends preserving schema source order in introspection lists. Field lists should follow their order in the schema source.

en.statement: A service may execute an unchanged request by reusing its earlier successful validation result.
en.explanation: The service can rely on an earlier successful validation result for an unchanged request, including its schema.

en.statement: In the September 2025 spec, a client may supply custom request metadata through an `extensions` map.
en.explanation: Request extensions reserve a map for implementation-specific information, with unrestricted contents.

en.statement: graphql.org says the reference implementation passes supplied field arguments as a resolver's `obj`.
en.explanation: graphql.org describes `obj` as the previous object, supplying the parent value for the field being resolved.

en.statement: A resolver may return a list whose individual item values resolve asynchronously.
en.explanation: GraphQL execution can await each list item's value before completing that item.

en.statement: The executor resolves included child fields after a resolver returns a non-null object value.
en.explanation: Completing an object value continues execution recursively through that object's sub-selection.

en.statement: For one object, the executor may execute each repeated selection of a response name separately.
en.explanation: Field collection groups a response name's selections into one field set, which the executor executes once for that object.

en.statement: Resolvers for fields nested beneath top-level mutation fields must be side-effect free.
en.explanation: Mutation side effects belong at its top level. Fields in its returned selection follow ordinary execution rules.

source.title: GraphQL specification: Normal and Serial Execution

en.statement: In a mutation, the next top-level field may start while the previous field's sub-selection runs.
en.explanation: Top-level mutation execution waits for the previous field and its selected subfields to finish before starting the next field.

source.title: GraphQL Specification: Normal and Serial Execution

en.statement: graphql.org says serial mutation execution rolls back earlier writes when a later field fails.
en.explanation: Serial mutation execution provides no built-in rollback; earlier successful changes can persist after a later field fails.

en.statement: After a client unsubscribes, the service may keep that subscription's source stream active.
en.explanation: Cancelling a subscription's response stream also cancels its source stream, providing a chance to clean up resources.

en.statement: The specification prescribes the transport protocol for a service's GraphQL execution requests.
en.explanation: The implementing service chooses the request transport; GraphQL's execution rules are independent of that choice.

en.statement: In the September 2025 spec, a service may answer a document that fails validation with `data: null`.
en.explanation: A validation failure produces a request error result, and the September 2025 spec says that result must not contain a data entry at all, not even null.

en.statement: For an execution that raises zero errors, a service includes an empty `errors` list in the response.
en.explanation: When execution completes without raising errors, the service omits the `errors` entry rather than returning an empty list.

en.statement: A service may place implementation-specific information under any keys in the response's `extensions` map.
en.explanation: The response's `extensions` entry holds a map for implementation-specific information. The spec imposes no further restrictions on that map's contents.

en.statement: A service may return completed sibling object fields when a nullable field raises an execution error.
en.explanation: A failure at a nullable field becomes null at that position while execution of its sibling fields continues, yielding partial data.

en.statement: A service stops null propagation at a failed Non-Null field's parent, even when that parent is Non-Null.
en.explanation: A Non-Null failure propagates through Non-Null ancestor positions until it reaches a nullable ancestor; that ancestor becomes null.

en.statement: A service adds another error entry when a field's original execution error propagates to its parent.
en.explanation: An execution error already recorded for a response position is not recorded again as its null result propagates upward.

en.statement: A service uses the field's aliased response name in the `path` of an execution error.
en.explanation: An error path identifies a response position, so its field segment uses the alias supplied by the operation.

en.statement: A service shortens an error's `path` to the nullable ancestor where null propagation stops.
en.explanation: After null propagation, an error's path still points to the field where the failure began, even if that field disappears from the returned data.

en.statement: A service uses line and column numbers starting at 1 when it supplies an error's `locations`.
en.explanation: An error's locations use one-based line and column positions for the beginning of an associated syntax element in the document.

en.statement: A service classifies a field-argument coercion failure during execution as a request error.
en.explanation: A field-argument coercion failure during execution is handled as an execution error at that field's response position.

en.statement: In the September 2025 spec, a client ignores unrecognized top-level entries in a GraphQL response.
en.explanation: Clients must ignore response entries beyond those this edition describes, allowing future protocol additions to coexist with existing clients.

en.statement: graphql.org recommends errors-as-data for expected business failures such as insufficient inventory.
en.explanation: Expected domain failures belong in schema-defined result types, letting clients discover their structure through introspection.

en.statement: graphql.org says clients should send a service's GraphQL requests over HTTP to one endpoint.
en.explanation: graphql.org uses one endpoint for a service because GraphQL exposes an entity graph rather than giving each resource its own URL.

en.statement: graphql.org says a client may send mutation operations over HTTP using GET.
en.explanation: graphql.org reserves GET for query operations; a client executes a mutation over HTTP with POST.

en.statement: graphql.org says a client's JSON POST `query` parameter over HTTP may hold a mutation document.
en.explanation: The JSON POST body's `query` parameter carries GraphQL document source text. Its name does not restrict that document to query operations.

en.statement: graphql.org recommends a server-error status over HTTP for a response with non-null `data` and errors.
en.explanation: graphql.org recommends a 2xx status when `data` is present and non-null, including responses that also contain errors.

en.statement: graphql.org recommends `application/graphql-response+json` in a client's `Accept` header over HTTP.
en.explanation: The `Accept` header advertises support for GraphQL's JSON response media type, helping the server choose a compatible response format.

en.statement: graphql.org says persisted documents store resolver results for clients to retrieve over HTTP.
en.explanation: graphql.org's persisted-document technique stores document text; the identifier replaces that text in the HTTP request.

en.statement: graphql.org recommends that servers authenticate clients over HTTP after validating GraphQL requests.
en.explanation: graphql.org places authentication middleware before GraphQL handling, so the request enters GraphQL with user and session information.

en.statement: graphql.org says servers should authorize fields during execution over HTTP so they can return partial data.
en.explanation: graphql.org delegates field authorization to business logic called by resolvers during execution. An authorization failure can therefore leave permitted data in the response.

en.statement: graphql.org recommends a smaller depth limit for nested lists than for other nested fields.
en.explanation: Nested lists can multiply the amount of returned data rapidly, so graphql.org suggests a separate, tighter list-nesting limit.

en.statement: graphql.org suggests base64-encoding pagination cursors to discourage clients from relying on their format.
en.explanation: Encoding reminds clients that cursors are opaque tokens. Clients pass them back to the service rather than depending on how the service represents a page position.

en.statement: graphql.org's pagination guide places the time a friendship begins on the friend node.
en.explanation: The pagination guide uses an edge for information about the relationship, such as friendship time. The node represents the object at that end of the relationship.

en.statement: The cursor connections spec uses last and after to page backward through a connection.
en.explanation: Backward pagination uses last with before. The server returns up to last edges that precede the before cursor.

en.statement: graphql.org says a server should return null from node(id:) for a deleted object.
en.explanation: The global object identification pattern asks a server to make a best effort to refetch the object. When that object is unavailable, node(id:) should yield null.

en.statement: graphql.org recommends continuous evolution of one schema as its approach to GraphQL API changes.
en.explanation: The Schema Design guide favors evolving a single schema over publishing API versions. This lets clients adopt new capabilities at their own pace.

en.statement: graphql.org's schema change guide lists adding a new interface implementation as a safe additive change.
en.explanation: The guide lists it among dangerous changes: fields returning that interface may start returning the new object type, so clients have to be ready for types they did not expect.

en.statement: graphql.org says adding an enum value is dangerous because clients may assume a fixed set.
en.explanation: An added enum value is structurally additive, yet a client may mishandle the new case. The Schema Change Management guide groups this under dangerous changes.

en.statement: graphql.org says parallel resolver execution automatically batches requests to an underlying data source.
en.explanation: Resolvers can issue separate requests to the data source. The guide describes collecting and dispatching them as a batch with a tool like DataLoader to address the N+1 problem.

en.statement: graphql.org recommends enabling GZIP on production services to compress GraphQL JSON responses.
en.explanation: GraphQL's JSON responses are largely text and compress well. The Performance guide encourages production services to enable GZIP for those responses.
